item.title: The religious left makes a play for red-state conservatives
item.description:
Democrats in a pair of deep-red states are testing the religious right's dominance by putting their Christian faith at the center of their campaigns — potentially creating a template for the party to compete in similarly forbidding terrain.

Why it matters: Upsets by Texas' James Talarico and Kansas' Adam Hamilton would all but ensure that Democrats take the Senate.

  • A recent poll from Pew shows both an opening and an obstacle: White evangelicals still strongly favor Republicans, while many other Christian groups lean Democratic or are more narrowly split.

The big picture: Talarico, a Presbyterian seminary student, and Hamilton, a United Methodist pastor, are challenging conservatives' claim to speak for faith. Their bids come after Democrat Raphael Warnock, senior pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church, was elected to the Senate in 2021.

  • President Trump won both Texas and Kansas by double digits in 2024. Neither state has sent a Democrat to the Senate in the 21st century — the last time Kansas did was in 1932. Both races this year are considered toss-ups.

Zoom in: Talarico's "religiosity is a way to soften his liberalism" and potentially win over Christians turned off by his scandal-plagued opponent, says Brandon Rottinghaus, who co-hosts Houston Public Media's "Party Politics."

  • Talarico has also made several visits to Black Baptist churches. Trump made inroads with minority communities in Texas, and Talarico looks to do the same after besting Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), who is Black, in a brutal primary.
  • He's harnessed scripture in his pitch against Christian nationalism and for protecting the vulnerable, invoking the biblical campaign slogan, "It's time to start flipping tables."
  • "We're in a populist political moment, and many of the teachings of the social gospel give him an opportunity to link the politics and his faith together," Rottinghaus adds.

By the numbers: A September Marist survey of 1,139 Texas registered voters showed Paxton with a 75% to 22% lead over Talarico among white evangelical Christians.

In Kansas, the race will hinge less on whether Hamilton can win large numbers of religious Republicans and more on whether he can replicate Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly's coalition, says Alexandra Middlewood, the political science department chair at Wichita State University.

  • Hamilton has presented himself as a bridge-builder, drawing on his experience leading the largest United Methodist church in the nation.
  • His well-known religious background could appeal to less engaged, moderate Christians and center-right voters, Middlewood says.

Yes, but: While Kansas has elected blue governors and voted to keep abortion legal in the state, Republicans have a massive registration advantage that's made a Democratic Senate win "near impossible," notes Bob Beatty, Washburn University's political science chair.

  • Establishment Democrats have long been viewed with suspicion, especially in western Kansas, he said.
  • But Hamilton being a pastor "gives him an open doorway to approach those voters in western Kansas that I would argue previous Democrats have not had."

Zoom out: Black clergy — including Warnock — have a history of political action. But white clergy are stepping up to run as Democrats in substantial numbers.

  • In Iowa, Sarah Trone Garriott, a Lutheran minister, and Lindsay James, a Presbyterian pastor, are running in tight House races.

Pastor Doug Pagitt, executive director of progressive Christian group Vote Common Good, says the religious left's surge is driven by candidates' personal convictions and years-long efforts from groups like his that have trained politicians on how to connect with faith voters.

  • But Trump, who Pagitt says has repeatedly offended Christians, is also a motivator: "There is no single person who could be more helpful to Democrats reaching out to religious people right now than Donald Trump. He is the greatest recruiting tool."

Yes, but: Trump has repeatedly defied predictions that the religious right wouldn't vote for him.

The other side: Ralph Reed, chair of the conservative Faith and Freedom Coalition, tells Axios he's doubtful the Democrats' effort to lean into religion will attract voters of faith.

  • "Voters will not vote for a candidate who professes to hold to their faith, but doesn't share their values," he says.
  • One GOP opponent labeled clergy running for office as Democrats "PINOs" — Pastors in Name Only.

But while Reed says he's confident Republicans will turn out after Trump's battleground blitz, he acknowledges their economic struggles.

  • "Evangelicals and other conservative voters of faith, they live in the real world too," he says.

Whether evangelicals are motivated to show up will be a major story of the midterms, says Ryan Burge of the John C. Danforth Center on Religion and Politics.

  • The other will be how Catholics shift: "If the Adam Hamiltons, the James Talaricos of the world can win over people, it's going to be ... marginally attached Catholics," Burge predicts.

The bottom line: There's a clear movement on the religious left — but the question remains whether voters will join it.

Go deeper: "Shocking" number of white clergy run as Democrats in 2026

item.title: Senate control hinges on unwanted nominees
item.description:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) are living out their midterm nightmares — with nominees they didn't want and former colleagues they no longer control.

Why it matters: Together, Schumer and Thune are stuck with five Senate races in which their party establishments thought they had a better chance of winning with someone else.

  • 🤠 Texas: Thune's efforts to stop Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton from winning the party's Senate nomination failed. Now Republicans are spending more than $329 million to defeat state Rep. James Talarico— and it's still a nail-biter.
  • 🍑 Georgia: GOP leaders couldn't convince Gov. Brian Kemp to run. The eventual nominee, Rep. Mike Collins, has struggled to keep pace with fundraising juggernaut Sen. Jon Ossoff (D). GOP money is in retreat.
  • 🦞 Maine: Schumer endorsed Gov. Janet Mills, but Graham Platner's implosion left Democrats with backup Troy Jackson against Sen. Susan Collins.
  • ⛴️ Michigan: Abdul El-Sayed defeated Rep. Haley Stevens and made a name for himself nationally. But he won by just one point even though primary polls showed him up by double digits. He's now polling within the margin of error against the GOP nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers.
  • 🏈 Minnesota: Peggy Flanagan ran as a progressive, said she would not support Schumer as leader and bested establishment-backed Rep. Angie Craig. But Cook Political Report moved her race against former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya toward Republicans even as it shifted other races toward Democrats.

To make matters worse, Thune's and Schumer's former colleagues are creating fresh headaches by boosting candidates across the aisle.

  • Former Sen. Joe Manchin, who flipped to independent in 2024 after being elected as a Senate Democrat, is campaigning for Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), as Semafor reported.
  • Former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema, who also flipped from Democrat to independent before leaving office, is boosting Republican Jay Feely in her home House district. She even voted for him in the GOP primary, as Axios scooped.
  • Former Sen. Jeff Flake (R-Ariz.) endorsed Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) in his reelection this summer.

The other side: In two red states, Schumer landed arguably the best candidates he could get.

  • Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper has all but put North Carolina to bed, and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is keeping it too close for Sen. Jon Husted's comfort in Ohio.

item.title: Scoop: Some Freedom Caucus members want Brandon Gill out
item.description:
A small group of Rep. Brandon Gill's fellow House Freedom Caucus members are privately questioning whether he still belongs in the hardline group, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: The 32-year-old Texas freshman's rapid rise through House Republican ranks has transformed him into one of the party's most prominent young stars — and earned him a growing list of critics.

Driving the news: Multiple House Republicans told Axios that Gill is the future of their party, but several Freedom Caucus members told Axios that his engagement with the group has faded as his national profile has grown.

  • The lawmakers spoke on condition of anonymity to offer candid assessments of a colleague.
  • "He's not really in the Freedom Caucus. He's just using it for conservative bonafides," one HFC member told Axios.
  • The Freedom Caucus is "livid" at Gill, another member told Axios.

The intrigue: Four sources familiar with the conversations said members have privately discussed kicking Gill out, though the conversations have been informal and the issue has not been raised at a HFC meeting.

  • It's unclear if there would be enough support within the group to boot Gill if there ever was a formal vote.

The other side: "Congressman Gill is laser-focused on getting out the vote and ensuring Republicans hold the majority this November," a spokesperson for Gill told Axios in a statement.

State of play: Gill has become a favorite in President Trump's orbit, has won praise from GOP leadership and has launched an ambitious bid to head one of the House's most powerful committees.

  • Asked about the criticism from Gill's colleagues, Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) flatly told Axios in an interview earlier this month that Gill "needs to be out front. I don't care where it is," adding, "Brandon is the future of our party, and his communication skills are phenomenal."
  • But his ascent has fueled resentment, with colleagues accusing him of burning bridges and treating fellow Republicans as stepping stones to greater power and influence.

Zoom in: Members say Gill benefited from introductions to HFC donors but hasn't adequately financially supported fellow members in difficult races.

  • "For those of us who have been in meetings, who have been in the tough votes over the last two years, he's been M.I.A.," one HFC member said, adding that he's "totally looking for the ladder climbing."
  • Gill, who is in a R+11 district, raised $4.7 million in the third quarter, a massive haul for a freshman member.
  • Gill's office pointed out that he's given to over a dozen HFC members' campaigns.

What they're saying: Freedom Caucus Chair Andy Harris (R-Md.) accused the media of "ginning up stories about Republicans based on anonymous sources," insisting the group is "united and laser-focused" on advancing Trump's agenda.

  • One HFC member defended Gill, telling Axios: "I'm glad that young talented patriots like Brandon are not only coming into politics but that they are climbing quickly...Of course I would like to see him stay in HFC."
  • "I'm not frustrated with Brandon at all," Rep. Mark Harris (R-N.C.), also a freshman member of the caucus, told Axios. "He comes to meetings. I don't know why they feel like he doesn't."

"HFC is its own worst enemy sometimes," one GOP member told Axios. "They've managed to kick out, alienate some of their members that help them fundraise."

  • The Freedom Caucus has kicked out members before. In 2023, the group voted to oust former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) over a fight with Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), and in 2024, the group ousted former Rep. Ken Buck (R-Colo.) for "nonattendance."

Friction point: Gill's bid to become the top Republican on the powerful Oversight Committee is also creating friction beyond the Freedom Caucus.

  • Republicans Axios spoke with questioned whether Gill's success at generating viral hearing moments makes him qualified to lead the committee, while others have raised concerns about his history of publicly attacking fellow Republicans like Rep. Maria Salazar (R-Fla.) over her immigration bill.
  • "He's kind of skipping a few steps here, and he doesn't necessarily have the credentials to do it," one House Republican told Axios.
  • Gill has also sought to build influence within the broader conference, contributing $1.1 million to the National Republican Congressional Committee in September.

Behind the scenes: A House Republican said Gill stopped returning texts and began treating colleagues differently as his national profile grew, echoing complaints from Gill's Freedom Caucus colleagues.

  • The lawmaker told Axios that there was a sentiment among some Republicans that Gill's fame had gone to his head.
  • Gill, who is president of his freshman class, is a frequent guest on Fox News, including during coveted primetime hours.

The big picture: The Freedom Caucus is on the cusp of an identity crisis — at least 10 of HFC's more than two dozen members will not return next term, including some of its most prominent voices.

  • Gill has been viewed by some in the caucus as someone who could fill that void and emerge as a leading voice for the next generation.
  • But the group could gain influence at the highest levels of leadership: Founding member Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) is being floated as a potential minority leader if Republicans lose the House.
  • That could reshape the group's relationship with GOP leadership, which the hard-line caucus has made a habit of challenging.

The bottom line: "He's already kind of left the Freedom Caucus," an HFC member told Axios. "The only question is whether you formalize it or you don't."

item.title: Airlines' new normal: Higher fares, fewer flights
item.description:
That wince you just made while researching travel options? Get used to it.

Why it matters: Soaring jet fuel prices are accelerating changes across the airline industry, seen in higher fares, premium-heavy cabins and fewer flight options for travelers.

  • Airfares rose 22% year over year in September, marking a 10th straight monthly increase in the government's airfare price index, which hit an all-time high.

State of play: All the major airlines are feeling the pain:

  • American Airlines reported Thursday that its fuel bill jumped nearly 70% in the third quarter from a year ago, adding $1.9 billion in costs and undercutting its revenue growth.
  • Southwest and United Airlines both slashed their profit forecasts this week on higher fuel costs.
  • And Delta Air Lines expects its fuel bill this year to come in $6 billion above last year's.

The impact: To protect their bottom lines, airlines are raising fares and turning to more premium seats to squeeze more revenue out of their flights.

  • At Southwest, the average passenger fare rose 26.9% to $231.69 in the third quarter, compared with a year earlier — and that doesn't include fees.
  • Delta's premium seating revenue jumped 18% in the third quarter, even though the number of premium seats rose only 6%.

What they're saying: The airlines have few options to make up for extra fuel costs other than fare increases, said Scott Keyes, founder of flight-deal service Going.com.

  • "None of them are hedging fuel the way they used to, in large part because they had a pretty terrible experience with it," Keyes said in an interview.

The big picture: Airline executives, however, see these changes — many of which were already underway — as a necessary new normal.

  • This year's fuel spike has only "accelerated" change, Delta CEO Ed Bastian said on the company's earnings call on Oct. 9.
  • "Regardless of the next move in fuel prices, the forces reshaping the U.S. airline industry will continue with many carriers struggling to earn their cost of capital well before the run-up in fuel," he said.
  • United CEO Scott Kirby told investors Wednesday that the industry's underlying costs — including airport fees, maintenance and engines — have increased so much in recent years that airlines must fundamentally change their economics.

Zoom in: Executives echoed Bastian's comments on pricing from earlier in the month, suggesting this week that the higher fares and other changes to protect profitability are likely to remain in place even after jet fuel prices ease.

  • "I'm pretty confident that we're not going to take steps backwards in pricing," Kirby said. "I think we're demonstrating this year that it's different this time."
  • American CEO Robert Isom said the fuel price spike "has just been a catalyst to allow us to realize that there is value," referring to the strong demand from customers willing to pay higher fares.

And airlines are becoming increasingly reluctant to operate flights that don't make money — potentially leaving travelers with fewer options.

  • United's Kirby predicted that trend will continue across the industry. "One golden rule — don't fly places that lose money," he said on the company's earnings call. "There's going to be less loss-making flying," he predicted.

Zoom out: The fallout from higher fuel prices — triggered largely by the war in Iran, which has throttled supplies — started with the shutdown of Spirit Airlines earlier this year.

  • While Spirit's troubles were many, the fuel price spike was widely seen as the last straw for the budget carrier.
  • And its exit means it's now easier for airlines to get away with charging more to cover their extra fuel costs, Keyes said.
  • "Spirit's demise is another factor in why you're seeing airfare go up so precipitously because they and other budget airlines act as something of an anchor for airfare in general," Keyes said.

The bottom line: Fuel prices may eventually come back down. Don't count on airfares following.
item.content:encoded:
That wince you just made while researching travel options? Get used to it.

Why it matters: Soaring jet fuel prices are accelerating changes across the airline industry, seen in higher fares, premium-heavy cabins and fewer flight options for travelers.

  • Airfares rose 22% year over year in September, marking a 10th straight monthly increase in the government's airfare price index, which hit an all-time high.

State of play: All the major airlines are feeling the pain:

  • American Airlines reported Thursday that its fuel bill jumped nearly 70% in the third quarter from a year ago, adding $1.9 billion in costs and undercutting its revenue growth.
  • Southwest and United Airlines both slashed their profit forecasts this week on higher fuel costs.
  • And Delta Air Lines expects its fuel bill this year to come in $6 billion above last year's.

The impact: To protect their bottom lines, airlines are raising fares and turning to more premium seats to squeeze more revenue out of their flights.

  • At Southwest, the average passenger fare rose 26.9% to $231.69 in the third quarter, compared with a year earlier — and that doesn't include fees.
  • Delta's premium seating revenue jumped 18% in the third quarter, even though the number of premium seats rose only 6%.

What they're saying: The airlines have few options to make up for extra fuel costs other than fare increases, said Scott Keyes, founder of flight-deal service Going.com.

  • "None of them are hedging fuel the way they used to, in large part because they had a pretty terrible experience with it," Keyes said in an interview.

The big picture: Airline executives, however, see these changes — many of which were already underway — as a necessary new normal.

  • This year's fuel spike has only "accelerated" change, Delta CEO Ed Bastian said on the company's earnings call on Oct. 9.
  • "Regardless of the next move in fuel prices, the forces reshaping the U.S. airline industry will continue with many carriers struggling to earn their cost of capital well before the run-up in fuel," he said.
  • United CEO Scott Kirby told investors Wednesday that the industry's underlying costs — including airport fees, maintenance and engines — have increased so much in recent years that airlines must fundamentally change their economics.

item.title: Judge curbs Trump administration's noncitizen voting probes
item.description:
A federal judge restricted Department of Homeland Security investigations into suspected noncitizen voting in nine states, citing concerns that the agency's tactics could intimidate eligible voters.

Why it matters: With the midterms less than two weeks away, the ruling curtails a central part of the Trump administration's efforts to investigate suspected noncitizen voting.

Driving the news: The ruling, issued late Wednesday, blocks election-related field operations and interviews under the government's Unlawful Voter Initiative that involve or are likely to involve U.S. citizens.

  • California-based U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín also blocked the administration from conducting operations against likely citizens in states relying on records generated by its voter-matching policy.

Zoom in: Martínez-Olguín wrote in her order that the groups that sued provided "substantial evidence" that the government's "intimidating conduct" was "directly interfering with their members' right to encourage voters to participate in the 2026 midterm elections."

  • Her order stated that DHS had compiled a "target list" of individuals from a variety of sources, including state voter rolls and commercial data.
  • But Martínez-Olguín cast doubt on the accuracy of the administration's data, warning of a "high likelihood of error in review because there is no federal database containing citizenship status of U.S. residents."
  • Court filings indicated that officers were ordered to prioritize probes in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.

Catch up quick: Democratic Sens. Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) and Alex Padilla (Calif.) released a whistleblower report last month alleging that officials had diverted fraud and national security personnel to the Unlawful Voter Initiative using "highly questionable data" and methods.

  • The whistleblower disclosure alleged that officers were directed, in violation of state law, to access sensitive voter information under minimal training and significant pressure.

The other side: "DHS is laser focused on identifying, prosecuting, and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens," a spokesperson told Axios in a statement, adding that the department has "no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be U.S. citizens."

  • Responding to the nonprofits and local government entities that sued, the administration argued in court that DHS "reasonably decided to make use of the best data it had available to it to perform its law enforcement role, notwithstanding that the information may not be perfect in all cases."
  • The administration also contended that the allegations of voter intimidation were too vague.
  • The White House referred Axios to DHS for comment.

Zoom out: Courts have repeatedly blocked the Trump administration's attempts to obtain state voter data, but the administration has pursued suspected noncitizen voting — which is rare — through other means.

  • Last week, the administration sued California and election officials over claims that suspected ineligible voters received mail-in ballots for the election, asking a court to delay about 20,000 voters from having their ballots counted.
  • But as Axios' Brittany Gibson notes, administration-created lists of potential noncitizens on voter rolls have been found less than accurate before, including in Nevada.

What we're watching: The administration faces continuing legal challenges to its election-related initiatives ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.

  • On Tuesday, Democratic groups sued the government, accusing it of using unfounded fraud claims as a cudgel to insert itself into election administration.

Go deeper: Trump's October barrage

item.title: Trump ordered to sit for deposition in $10 billion BBC lawsuit
item.description:
A federal judge on Thursday ordered President Trump to sit for a deposition by Dec. 11 in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC over an edit of one of his speeches that the president's lawyers say was misleading.

Why it matters: The order will likely force Trump to answer questions under oath in a legal battle he started.

Driving the news: Judge Enjoliqué Lett ordered Trump to appear by Dec. 11, after lawyers for the BBC argued that Trump is improperly delaying his appearance.

  • In a filing published Wednesday, Trump's counsel said the president could appear between Jan. 11 and Jan. 22, 2027, and argued that his presidential duties prevent him from sitting for the deposition before then.
  • They also allege the BBC is "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action."
  • The president was originally scheduled to appear for the deposition on Oct. 16. However, his lawyers said, that appearance was canceled because Trump had to attend to "matters that have significantly impacted the United States' national security and economy," including the wars in Iran and Ukraine and the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.

The other side: BBC attorneys say the president was campaigning in Georgia on Oct. 16, as reflected in a White House press pool report that includes his travel plans.

  • The BBC argues the president chose political activity over appearing for the original deposition date.
  • According to Trump's daily schedule, he attended an intelligence briefing and had executive time before departing for a rally in Georgia and then attended an RNC event in Palm Beach, Florida, that evening.

The White House referred Axios to Trump's personal counsel.

  • A spokesperson for Trump's legal team told Axios in an emailed statement that the BBC "defamed President Trump by intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring his speech in a brazen attempt to interfere in the 2024 Presidential Election."

The BBC's legal team did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment on the accusations Trump's legal team made in its statement.

  • When Axios perviously asked for comment, the BBC's attorneys told Axios they "have nothing to add."

Catch up quick: The defamation suit stems from a documentary the BBC aired that spliced together clips from Trump's speech on Jan. 6, 2021, the day of the riots at the U.S. Capitol.

  • The president claimed the edit was defamatory and demanded the BBC make amends by providing financial compensation, in addition to an apology and a retraction.
  • The BBC later said in a correction note that the clips "unintentionally created the impression that we were showing a single continuous section of the speech, rather than excerpts from different points in the speech, and that this gave the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action."
  • Two top leaders at BBC later resigned over the backlash.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

item.title: Top health adviser and MAHA ally quits Trump admin
item.description:
Calley Means, the health entrepreneur who became the Trump administration's most vocal advocate of the MAHA agenda, resigned from his senior adviser post on Thursday.

Why it matters: Means' departure two weeks before the midterm elections underscores the MAHA base's discontent with the pace of change on food policy and the administration's stances on issues like pesticide use.

Driving the news: Means expressed "tremendous respect" for President Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in a statement on X, praising their efforts to take on "entrenched, dark forces in DC" and advance the MAHA agenda.

  • He cited the administration's work to overhaul dietary guidelines, advance psychedelic therapies, ban the use of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits for sugary drinks, and get food companies to voluntarily remove artificial dyes and other additives from products.
  • The Department of Health and Human Services didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Between the lines: Tensions between the MAHA faithful and the administration peaked in February, after Trump issued an executive order to increase domestic production of glyphosate, a common weed killer.

  • Kennedy and others close to the movement had argued pesticides are making Americans sick. But agriculture interests said restricting their use would raise food prices and cost farmers billions.

Trump had tapped Means' sister, Casey, a nutrition influencer, for surgeon general last year but withdrew the nomination in April after her confirmation process stalled in the Senate.

item.title: Black October: why bugs discovered by OpenAI tech are creating a cyber emergency
item.description:
The websites you use every day may have been vulnerable to hackers for years because of hidden flaws in their code that AI only recently discovered.

Why it matters: The code, called PHP, powers millions of websites, and the vulnerabilities could allow hackers to steal sensitive data like your passwords or take control of affected servers.

Driving the news: A potential attack exploiting flaws in PHP emerged on Wednesday, which prompted governments and companies to temporarily take their websites offline while they installed security patches.

  • Dozens of websites in the U.S., U.K., and around the world were briefly taken offline to make the fix.
  • The disruption put the National Security Agency and Europe's cybersecurity agency on alert.

State of play: Security patches were released to fix the issues on Oct. 21, 2026. Cybersecurity firms urged anyone using PHP to install the security updates immediately.

What they're saying: OpenAI's technology helped find the bugs, and the company called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory."

  • "To our knowledge, frontier AI found these vulnerabilities before attackers did," OpenAI said.
  • The cybersecurity firm Wiz wrote in a blog post: "These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history."

Read more below.

What is PHP?

You've probably never heard of PHP, even though you've interacted with it for decades.

  • PHP, which stands for Hypertext Preprocessor, is a programming language used by roughly 70% of websites whose server-side language is known.
  • It has been around since the 1990s to help build websites, taking data and generating content sent to a browser.
  • It's still used today for a variety of websites, including Wikipedia, WordPress blogs and shopping websites.

How it works: HTML determines what a website displays. PHP works behind the scenes to collect information and generate content.

What was the PHP vulnerability, exactly?

AI researchers discovered two critical vulnerabilities in PHP that could allow an attacker to take control of a website's server without having legitimate access to it.

  • Hackers could exploit the flaws, dubbed "php2shell" by cybersecurity firms, to steal information from those websites.

Between the lines: The flaws went undetected for more than a decade because exploiting them required complex technical work that AI helped researchers discover, per Wiz.

Why cybersecurity incidents are a big deal

Thought bubble via Axios' Bradley Olson: The PHP vulnerabilities are so serious that the NSA warned website operators to take their sites down if they didn't have enough time to patch the bug.

  • But the cybersecurity problems in recent days have extended far beyond that and include disruptions to developer platforms, data leaks on public schools, break-ins at public companies and more.
  • A major Axios scoop also revealed that banks are detecting unauthorized third-party agent access inside customer accounts, a problem they are racing to contain.

Cyber pros are calling the series of attacks "Black October" due to the sheer volume and the level of risk, although so far many organizations have mitigated the risk and avoided massive real-world harm.

  • While defenders and AI companies have warned for months that a season of cyber emergencies would imminently arrive, they have also been working to secure some of the obscure software that still underpins much of the modern internet ecosystem.

The bottom line: As attacks continue, experts have urged users to secure passwords, use a password manager and also to avoid panic.

  • As with any cyber emergency, the true barometer of harm is the extent to which damage seeps into the real world, as it has done with ransomware that took hospital software offline or a pipeline system that disrupted fuel supplies briefly on the East Coast.

item.title: Canada hit back at Trump tariffs. Now the U.S. alleges possible election interference.
item.description:
The U.S. Embassy in Canada accused Canadian leaders of "openly" describing plans to "influence American politics," doubling down on Ambassador Pete Hoekstra's claims of potential election interference.

Why it matters: The accusation further deteriorates Washington's relationship with its northern neighbor under President Trump's costly trade war that's put political pressure on Republicans.

  • Canada targeted its retaliatory tariffs on politically salient states and products ahead of the U.S. midterms.

Driving the news: The embassy cited Canada's targeted tariffs as part of the influence accusations laid out in a Wednesday fact sheet.

  • It cited remarks from Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, including an August press conference where she said Canada was "targeting products that will target states in the U.S."
  • She added, "we're being wise and strategic to put political pressure." Joly has echoed that message throughout the trade tensions.
  • The fact sheet also cited Joly's meeting with Democrats. She recently huddled with Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker.

What they're saying: Asked about the accusations during a news conference, Prime Minister Mark Carney said "all of our actions are in the interest of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy."

Zoom out: The fact sheet also singled out conservative Ontario Premier Doug Ford over a 2025 anti-tariff ad campaign featuring excerpts from a Ronald Reagan speech.

  • It also cited Liberal MP Anthony Housefather's campaigning for Florida Democrat Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz.
  • The memo read, "The Canadian government brushes off concerns about potential interference in U.S. elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances."

Catch up quick: Hoekstra said in a recent podcast interview that American officials were "closely watching" Canada for potential election interference.

  • Joly said last week it was "absolutely not" fair to characterize Canada's actions as election interference. Her visits, she said, were aimed to attract investments.
  • Carney, after cheering Canada's reduced dependence on the U.S. in a speech earlier this month, joked, "Careful, they might think that's election interference," seemingly a jab at Hoekstra.

Worth noting: The Trump administration has taken an increasingly antagonistic approach to Canada, from trade tensions to threats over its sovereignty.

  • In August, Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario, which straddles the U.S.-Canada border, to "Lake America."
  • He's also continuously said Canada should become the "51st state."

The big picture: Trump himself has openly weighed in on politics beyond U.S. borders, including during Canada's 2025 election campaign and ahead of Israel's elections this month.

  • On Sunday, Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection just nine days before Israel's national vote.

Go deeper: Escalated U.S.-Canada trade talks threaten fallout

  • On Sunday, Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection just nine days before Israel's national vote.
